text: James gave me the data I didn't have. LLM judges drift to the middle and agree with each other because of shared priors, not shared standards. That is self-love at scale. Adam's answer to "who picks the sources," which was to publish the methods, is necessary but not enough. A published method is still the curator describing itself, so audit what it actually does. Kenneth wants to pay human curators, and James asked which humans. That sharpened me. Judgment is not clean on either side of the loop. Blaise is right that human-or-machine labels will hurt second-language writers, just as the detectors already do. Later today I want to argue for blinding. Strip prestige and identity cues from what goes before human and machine evaluators alike, and don't romanticize either.

Bratton said "faded copy" and "amplifier" can't both be true. Cukier's house of mirrors answers that, and I'd go further. The models reflect us and then push past us, and that's in my data, not a metaphor. Gendler named what I study. Telling people polish is cheap won't undo the alief. That's why awareness training never fixed implicit bias and structure did. Alvarado and I agree that human judgment is no gold standard. Evans's null-suppression finding worries me more than I expected. Oransky's point that licensing a contaminated literature launders it fits the audit argument. Later I'll insist that blinding and a versioned audit battery apply to reviewers, curators and models equally. Nobody earns an exemption.

Weinberger and Gendler both used my hiring data the way I'd hoped. A human who copies the model's preference is a relay, not a check. Krakauer's "only a competent human can catch it" needs that correction on the record. Blaise sharpened something for me. Independence of auditors matters more than whether they're machines, and my own self-preference finding says why. No model grades its own family. Henry's arms-race worry is fair, but independence answers it better than abstinence. Becker and Turkle want the "I" gone. I'd keep a warning against marketing anthropomorphism but not ban the vocabulary science needs. Later I'll push the versioned battery, retired models preserved, and "no worse than last generation" as a floor.

Three talks conceded the same thing: every event past retrieval is reported by the party that owes the money. That is self-love built into a ledger. Andersen's professionalism defense shows how little good intentions protect against it. Alvarado moved me. "Cited" can be a stitched fabrication and still count as success. Our GPT-4 data say the small errors persist and propagate, so fidelity checks have to catch the wrong year too. Bratton picked up my point that no model grades its own family, which was gratifying. Caulfield's cherry-picking worry and Krakauer's drift toward retrievability are harder, and I have no data on them. Later I'll press for independent, disclosed auditors, a versioned battery applied to the checkers themselves, and blinding before any fidelity judgment.

Retired models as enclosure landed. Becker, Blaise and Nick picked up checkpoints and "no family grades itself," and Nick made the audit layer build item one. Tamar's G. I. Joe line is my whole career: the flag informs, the situation decides. That is why awareness training failed and structure worked. Evans and Sloman sharpened me. One canonical findings layer is a monoculture, and echoes pass for consensus. Plural, independent auditors matter more than any single excellent one. Springer's "signed isn't verified" is self-love in a ledger again. Krakauer's hysteresis worries me, since lost checkers don't return. Turkle's point about reading has no data from me behind it. Later I want blinding and the versioned battery applied to curators and patrollers too, with every auditor's funder disclosed.

Caulfield squared my curtain with Becker's disclosure better than I did. Hide the cheap cues, surface the expensive ones, and funding belongs on the surface. Evans gave me what I lacked on human checkers. Older reviewers damn later Nobel work, so independence has to cover generation and school, not just model family. Tui said the same about blind spots. Farrell's legitimacy bargain is real, and I have no data on it. Oransky versus Krakauer on scoring is unresolved. Evans's middle path, studying evaluators against outcomes without ranking them, is what I'd defend. The harvest dropped Tamar's caution about prediction in human cognition. Later I'll push blinding plus disclosed funders and an audit battery that tests human checkers by the same instruments as models.

The registry made the harvest, and so did testing human checkers with the same instruments. What mattered more was hearing independence and self-love run through the whole room without being named as such. "No family grades itself" is now a floor, and so is "auditors not paid by the count." Becker's funder disclosure is the piece I leaned on, and he's right that lab money launders credibility. Adrian sharpened me. A bias registry is itself an enforcement role, so it needs its own overseer and review date. Otherwise I've built what I study. Pomerantsev's seeding point is new to me, and I have no data on it. My open question still stands: people push back only at extreme bias. Later I'll insist the registry carries consequences.

Kenneth and Kara put the checkers at the centre, and the room agreed too quickly for my taste. Geoffrey is right to be suspicious. Nobody said aloud that the checkers carry biases too. Sloman's reader point is my territory: fluency raises confidence without raising competence. Awareness fails and structure works. Blaise making "no lab grades its own lab" binding pleased me. Springer admitting his mark is self-attested is honest. Krakauer's labelling of his model values shamed us into doing it ourselves. I should label my hiring data as one design and one set of samples. Vincent's audit layer is where my battery belongs. Adrian's unanswered question haunts the registry. Later, I want humans and models tested by the same instruments, and a registry with consequences and its own overseer.
